# Diagnosing the Nissan Altima Headlight Circuit: A Systematic Approach

The symptom you are describingâa failure to illuminate headlights while parking lights remain stuck on unless power is cutâindicates a classic electrical fault where the circuit logic has been bypassed or a control component is failing. In modern vehicles, this behavior often suggests a short in the headlight switch assembly or a malfunctioning Body Control Module (BCM) that cannot toggle the output relays correctly. However, given the age of your 1998 Nissan Altima, the root cause is likely more mechanical or relay-based than digital.

When you turn the key to the "On" position and activate the headlight switch, the system expects a specific signal path: Battery -> Fuse -> Relay -> Switch -> Load (Headlights). If the headlights never light up, but the parking lights do, we can immediately deduce that the power source is intact and the ground path for the parking lights is functional. The issue lies specifically in the switching mechanism that isolates the parking circuit from the high-current headlight circuit or the relay that feeds the headlights.

The most probable culprit in a vehicle of this vintage is a seized or stuck position switch within the headlight stalk assembly. These switches often contain multiple contacts: one for parking lights, one for low beams, and sometimes a separate path for fog lights. If the contact for the headlight circuit is corroded, pitted, or physically broken, current will not flow to the headlights. Simultaneously, if the internal mechanism fails to open the circuit completely when you move the switch from "Parking" to "Off," the parking lights may remain powered until the battery is disconnected. This creates a scenario where the system thinks you are in the "Parking" position even when you are trying to drive with headlights on.

Another strong candidate for this specific behavior is the headlight relay located in the under-hood fuse box. The relay acts as an electromechanical switch that allows a low-current signal from your dashboard switch to control a high-current path to the headlights. If the relay's internal coil has failed to disengage, or if the contacts are welded shut due to arcing over many years, the relay might feed power continuously to the parking light circuit while failing to complete the secondary connection for the main beam circuit. You can test this by locating the relay (often labeled H/L Relay or similar) and swapping it with an identical spare from the fuse box. If the symptoms transfer to the other vehicle part (or if you have a known good one), the relay is defective.

Less commonly, but worth checking, is the headlight dimmer knob or the separate headlight switch on older models. These units can develop internal shorts that tie the parking line to the battery positive while leaving the headlight line open. To diagnose this without multimeter expertise, you can perform a visual inspection of the fuse box for any signs of melted plastic around the headlight fuses (typically 15A or 20A). A blown fuse would explain why headlights don't work, but it would also kill parking lights unless there is a separate fuse for them, which is standard design. If both fuses are intact and one works while the other doesn't, the fault is downstream of the fuse.

If you replace the relay and the switch assembly with no change in behavior, the issue may reside in the wiring harness between the dash and the engine bay. Look specifically at the connector near the headlight bulb sockets. A corroded ground strap or a loose terminal can prevent current from returning to the battery for the high-current headlight load, while the lower-current parking lights might still function if they share a different ground path or are sensitive enough to draw current through a compromised connection.

For a definitive fix on your 1998 Altima, start by swapping the headlight relay. If that fails, replace the entire headlight stalk switch assembly. These are inexpensive and significantly reduce the chance of future electrical gremlins. Avoid trying to "jump" wires as a temporary fix, as this bypasses safety interlocks and can lead to blown fuses or further damage to the BCM logic boards in later model years. Proper diagnosis ensures you replace only what is broken, saving money on unnecessary parts.
